Could someone explain to me the meaning of the planck length? I still don't really understand why it's the smallest anything can be.

The following has been taken from this link and does a good job of explaining this:

http://www.quora.com/Why-do-physicists-think-that-the-Planck-length-is-the-smallest-possible-length

"I won't really say that physicists think that the Planck length is the smallest possible length, but rather that they think that speaking of a length smaller than the Planck length is completely meaningless within the frameworks currently available to us. This is rather akin to modelling an array of particles as a continuum. It wouldn't make sense to talk of distance scales smaller than the spacing between the particles in the continuum model because the model breaks down in that limit but obviously that doesn't mean that such distances don't exist. So, while classically speaking you can have curvature singularities in your solutions to the Einstein field equations of gravity, you don't actually expect such singularities to show up in Nature since interesting quantum effects are going to be kicking in by the time the curvature gets in the vicinity of the inverse Planck length squared. Planck length is the fundamental length scale in a quantum theory of gravity much in the same way the inverse of the electron mass is the fundamental length scale for electron-photon scattering.

That said, there is reason to believe that the Universe is granulated at the Planck scale. When you measure energy and temperature in the same units by setting the Boltzmann constant to unity, entropy becomes a dimensionless quantity just like its counterpart in information theory due to Shannon. Roughly speaking, entropy measures the amount of information you have in a system. That is to say, if you had to compress everything you know about a system into as few (qu)bits as possible, you would need a number of bits equal to the entropy on an average. Now, in the context of black holes, there is an associated entropy proportional to the area of the event horizon of the black hole, as shown by Hawking and Bekenstein. The entropy is dimensionless, but the area is not, so you'll have to choose special units in which to measure the area. As it turns out, the entropy is the number of Planck areas in the event horizon. So, we could say that the degrees of freedom of the Universe i.e. the input we would have to give to a supercomputer to simulate the Universe, dwells in two dimensions and that there is one such degree in every Planck-sized cell.

Addendum: So, what if we take into consideration all the quantum effects? Will it then make sense to talk of sub-Planck length scales? String theory, which is a quantum theory of gravity amongst other things offers an interesting answer. There is a correspondence called the T-duality that relates different descriptions of the same observable physics. As it turns out physics at say ten times the Planck length is indistinguishable from physics at one-tenth the Planck length. So, in that sense, we are really not going to see anything new at sub-Planck distances. We just get our everyday physics but seen through a different window."
